paragraphs.heading: Division by hand
paragraphs.text: Long division is the standard way to divide numbers with many digits using only pencil and paper. It turns one hard division into a chain of easy steps, so even very large numbers can be handled. The number being divided is the dividend, the number you divide by is the divisor, and the answer is the quotient. When the divisor has a single digit, people nearly always use a shorter form called short division.

paragraphs.heading: The basic loop
paragraphs.text: First, divide the divisor into the left-most digit of the dividend. The whole-number part of that answer becomes the first digit of the result, and a subtraction gives what is left over. That leftover is carried along: you bring down the next digit of the dividend beside it and repeat. The work ends when every digit has been used and nothing is left over.

paragraphs.heading: Dividing 500 by 4
paragraphs.text: Four goes into 5 once, so write 1 above the 5, multiply 1 by 4, and subtract to leave 1. Bring down the next 0 to make 10. Four goes into 10 twice, giving 8, and 10 minus 8 leaves 2. Bring down the last 0 to make 20, and 4 goes into 20 five times with nothing left. The quotient reads 125.

paragraphs.heading: Remainders and decimals
paragraphs.text: If something is left at the end, you can write the answer as the quotient plus a fraction: the remainder over the divisor. Or you can keep going by writing the dividend as 500.000 and bringing down zeros past the units digit, with the decimal point in the answer placed right above the one in the dividend. Steps that would only give a leading zero can be skipped. If the first digit is 1 and the divisor is 4, you start with the first two digits, 12; with a divisor of 13, you would start with 127.

paragraphs.heading: The bus stop
paragraphs.text: In English-speaking countries, long division is not written with ∕ or ÷. Instead it is set out as a table: a right parenthesis or vertical bar separates the divisor from the dividend, and a bar drawn over the dividend separates it from the quotient. Together these marks are sometimes called the division bracket, or even the bus stop. The layout grew in the 18th century out of an older one-line notation.

paragraphs.heading: Where it came from
paragraphs.text: Related methods go back to the 12th century. Al-Samawal al-Maghribi worked with decimal numbers in ways that need long division, though he never set out the procedure. The earliest printed example comes from Caldrini in 1491, where it was called the Danda method. The exact procedure taught today was introduced by Henry Briggs around 1600.

paragraphs.heading: In classrooms today
paragraphs.text: Cheap calculators and computers now do most division at school and at work. In North America, long division has been played down or partly dropped as part of reform mathematics, which stresses understanding and technology. Countries such as Japan and Germany still teach and practise it in primary school.
